paragraphs: Yaakov Termosera is mentioned in Jerusalem Talmud Berakhot 2:3. Hyman places him in the time of Rabbi Yochanan. Hyman understands the Arukh’s entry for Tormusar as referring to a bathhouse and suggests that the name may reflect work as a bath attendant.

notes.text: The Jerusalem Talmud tractate is not supplied. The bathhouse/bath-attendant explanation remains tentative.

The saved whole Guggenheimer Berakhot2:3 scalar contains עד יעקב תרמוסרה in Rabbi Yochanan’s bath/tefillin narrative. This identifies a matching tractate beside Hyman’s unspecified chapter2halakhah3. It does not decide person versus building or place. The Arukh lemma was not newly inspected; Hyman owns the bathhouse explanation and tentative bath-attendant suggestion. Heading Termosera and lemma Tormusar remain different supplied spellings; the old note’s misquote ולי is superseded by actual ואולי.

The printed Arukh, p. 280, quotes Jerusalem Talmud Maaser Sheni under תורמוסר and glosses it as “the proprietor of the bathhouse,” distinguishing him from the bathhouse attendant. The editorial addition discusses the Berakhot expression in terms of the heat of the bath. Penei Moshe reads the phrase in Berakhot as referring to a house next to the bathhouse, while Jastrow reads it as referring to Jacob the bathkeeper or attendant. Hyman’s occupational interpretation is a suggestion.
